facts.fact: Sanskar Kendra is a museum in Ahmedabad, India, designed by Le Corbusier.
facts.quote: Sanskar Kendra is a museum at Ahmedabad, India, designed by the architect Le Corbusier.

facts.fact: It was planned as part of a larger Cultural Centre for Ahmedabad, but only the museum was built; its foundation stone was laid on 9 April 1954.
facts.quote: But out of whole planned cultural centre, only museum was built. Its foundation stone was laid on 9 April 1954.

facts.fact: The building stands on Le Corbusier's signature pilotis, 3.4 metres high.
facts.quote: It rests on his signature pilotis, that are 3.4 metres (11 ft) high there.

facts.fact: Its exterior is plain brick with exposed raw concrete (béton brut) structure on a 7-metre grid.
facts.quote: The building's exterior is of plain brick with exposed elements of raw concrete (Béton brut) structure. The structural grid is 7 metres (23 ft).

facts.fact: The building is designed to protect against the hot climate, with large basins on the roof originally meant as planters.
facts.quote: The building is designed to protect against the hot climate.  On the roof there are several large basins originally intended as planters.

facts.fact: Visitors enter from underneath, into an open court with a large pool and a ramp up to the exhibition spaces.
facts.quote: One enters from underneath the building where there is an open court with a large pool and a ramp that leads to the exhibition spaces.

facts.fact: Like Le Corbusier's museums in Tokyo and Chandigarh, its plan is based on a spiral and designed to be expanded.
facts.quote: The museum is similar to other museum projects by Le Corbusier, such as the "Museum of unlimited extension" project, the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo, and the Government Museum and Art Gallery in Chandigarh, in that the plan is based on a spiral and is designed to be expanded.

facts.fact: The museum closed in March 2020 and has since been kept closed for renovation.
facts.quote: The museum was closed in March 2020 following the COVID-19 pandemic. It was kept closed for renovation since.

facts.fact: The NGV, founded in 1861 in Melbourne, is Australia's oldest and most visited art museum.
facts.quote: The National Gallery of Victoria, popularly known as the NGV, is an art museum in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia. Founded in 1861, it is Australia's oldest and most visited art museum.

facts.fact: The NGV International building, designed by Roy Grounds, opened in 1968, was redeveloped by Mario Bellini and reopened in 2003; it is on the Victorian Heritage Register.
facts.quote: The NGV International building, designed by Sir Roy Grounds, opened in 1968, and was redeveloped by Mario Bellini before reopening in 2003. It houses the gallery's international art collection and is on the Victorian Heritage Register.

facts.fact: Grounds kept the commission after splitting from his partners Frederick Romberg and Robin Boyd in 1962, and designed the gallery at 180 St Kilda Road.
facts.quote: In 1962, Roy Grounds split from his partners, Frederick Romberg and Robin Boyd, retained the commission, and designed the gallery at 180 St Kilda Road (now known as NGV International).

facts.fact: The bluestone-clad building was completed in December 1967 and officially opened on 20 August 1968.
facts.quote: The new bluestone clad building was completed in December 1967, and Victorian Premier Henry Bolte officially opened it on 20 August 1968.

facts.fact: Its Leonard French stained-glass ceiling, one of the world's largest pieces of suspended stained glass, casts coloured light on the floor below, and the water-wall entrance is another well-known feature.
facts.quote: One of the features of the building is the Leonard French stained-glass ceiling, one of the world's largest pieces of suspended stained glass, which casts colourful light on the floor below. The water-wall entrance is another well-known feature of the building.

facts.fact: The building is surrounded by a moat and fountains.
facts.quote: The building is surrounded by a moat and fountains, while the main entrance features a famous water wall, which has been used to display the art of Keith Haring and others.

facts.fact: Bellini's redevelopment created all new galleries, keeping only the exterior, the central courtyard and the Great Hall.
facts.quote: The design was extensive, creating all new galleries while leaving only the exterior, the central courtyard and Great Hall intact.

facts.fact: After public protests organised by the National Trust of Victoria, the redesign kept a water wall, set slightly forward of the original.
facts.quote: The plans included doing away with the water wall, but following public protests organised by the National Trust of Victoria, the design was altered to include a new one slightly forward of the original.

facts.fact: Luis Barragán planned Torres de Satélite in 1957, an urban sculpture made with the sculptor Mathias Goeritz.
facts.quote: In 1957 he planned Torres de Satélite (an urban sculpture created in collaboration with sculptor Mathias Goeritz) and an exclusive residential area, Las Arboledas, a few kilometers away from Ciudad Satélite.

facts.fact: The towers date from 1957–58.
facts.quote: Torres de Satélite, Mexico City (1957–58), in collaboration with Mathias Goeritz

facts.fact: The Torres de Satélite stand in the middle of the Periférico, Mexico City's main freeway.
facts.quote: The Torres de Satélite (Satellite Towers) landmark stands in the middle of Periferico, Mexico City's main freeway.

facts.fact: Designed by Goeritz and Barragán and inspired by ideas of the painter Jesús Reyes Ferreira, they are a significant work of modern sculpture and architecture.
facts.quote: Designed by Mathias Goeritz and Luis Barragán and inspired by the painter Jesus Reyes Ferreyra's ideas, it is a significant piece of modern sculpture and architecture.

facts.fact: Because ownership of the site was unclear, no government maintained the towers and they fell into disrepair; in the late 1990s they were repainted in their original colours, chosen by Barragán.
facts.quote: As ownership of the site where they were built is unclear, they were not maintained by any government and fell into disrepair. In the late 1990s, they were repainted in their original colors, which had been chosen by Barragán.

facts.fact: Ciudad Satélite, the suburb the towers are named for, was first conceived as a satellite city, a commuter community outside Mexico City.
facts.quote: Satélite was originally conceived as a satellite city, a commuter-bedroom community that developers hoped to maintain as a greenbelt between it and Mexico City itself; however, rapid development (and subsequent real estate market increases) made this untenable.

facts.fact: Radio City Music Hall is an entertainment venue and theatre at 1260 Avenue of the Americas, within Rockefeller Center in Midtown Manhattan.
facts.quote: Radio City Music Hall (also known as Radio City) is an entertainment venue and theater at 1260 Avenue of the Americas, within Rockefeller Center, in the Midtown Manhattan neighborhood of New York City.

facts.fact: It was designed by Edward Durell Stone and Donald Deskey in the Art Deco style.
facts.quote: Radio City Music Hall was designed by Edward Durell Stone and Donald Deskey in the Art Deco style.

facts.fact: It was built on land first meant for a Metropolitan Opera house and opened on 27 December 1932 as part of Rockefeller Center.
facts.quote: Radio City Music Hall was built on a plot of land that was originally intended for an opera house for the Metropolitan Opera, plans for which were canceled in 1929. It opened on December 27, 1932, as part of the construction of Rockefeller Center.

facts.fact: Its four-tiered auditorium was the world's largest when it opened.
facts.quote: Radio City's four-tiered auditorium was the world's largest when it opened.

facts.fact: The theatre's promoter, Roxy, wanted red seats and an oval auditorium, because oval halls were then thought to have better acoustics.
facts.quote: Roxy wanted red seats because he believed it would make the theater successful, and he wished for the auditorium to be oval in shape because contemporary wisdom held that oval auditoriums had better acoustic qualities.

facts.fact: Stone faced the building in Indiana limestone, like the rest of Rockefeller Center.
facts.quote: Stone used Indiana limestone for the facade, as with all the other buildings in Rockefeller Center, but he also included some distinguishing features.

facts.fact: Its Art Deco decoration, with sharp lines, broke with the ornate rococo ornament usual in movie palaces of the time.
facts.quote: Designed by Edward Durell Stone, the theater had Art Deco decoration, whose sharp lines represented a break with the traditional ornate rococo ornament associated with movie palaces at the time.

facts.fact: It became a New York City Landmark in May 1978 and was extensively renovated in 1999.
facts.quote: Radio City was designated a New York City Landmark in May 1978, and it was restored and allowed to remain open. The theater was extensively renovated in 1999.

facts.fact: The Pulitzer Arts Foundation is an art museum in St. Louis's Grand Center Arts District, designed by Tadao Ando.
facts.quote: Known informally as the Pulitzer, the museum is located at 3716 Washington Boulevard in the Grand Center Arts District. The building is designed by the internationally renowned Japanese architect Tadao Ando.

facts.fact: Completed in October 2001 after four years of construction and nearly ten of planning, it was Ando's first public building in the United States.
facts.quote: Completed in October 2001 after four years of construction and nearly ten of planning, the Pulitzer Arts Foundation was the first public building in United States to be designed by architect Tadao Ando, who won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1995.

facts.fact: The building shows Ando's attention to light and water and his signature use of concrete.
facts.quote: The building is characterized by Ando's longstanding attention to natural elements such as light and water, as well as his signature use of concrete.

facts.fact: Its concrete was cast on site using advanced techniques that were uncommon in America at the time.
facts.quote: The concrete forms that comprise the building were cast on site during a nearly four-year construction period using advanced techniques that  were uncommon in America at the time.

facts.fact: In 2014–15 the lower level was turned into two new public galleries, raising public space from 6,800 to about 10,400 square feet.
facts.quote: In consultation with Ando and his office, the Pulitzer increased the public space in the building from 6,800 square feet to roughly 10,400  square feet and reopened on May 1, 2015, with three concurrent solo exhibitions of artists Alexander Calder, Fred Sandback and Richard Tuttle.

facts.fact: Ellsworth Kelly's Blue Black, a 28-foot wall sculpture, hangs beneath a skylight in the main gallery.
facts.quote: Ellsworth Kelly’s Blue Black is a twenty-eight-foot vertical wall sculpture beneath a skylight in the building’s main gallery.

facts.fact: Works are shown without wall labels to encourage unmediated encounters with art.
facts.quote: Works at the Pulitzer are installed without the wall labels to encourage unmediated encounters with art.

facts.fact: The Supreme Court of Canada Building stands just west of Parliament Hill at 301 Wellington Street, Ottawa.
facts.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada Building (French: édifice de la Cour suprême du Canada) is located just west of Parliament Hill, at 301 Wellington Street.

facts.fact: It sits on a bluff high above the Ottawa River and is home to the Supreme Court of Canada.
facts.quote: It is situated on a bluff high above the Ottawa River in downtown Ottawa and is home to the Supreme Court of Canada.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1938, and the cornerstone was laid in May 1939 by Queen Elizabeth, consort of King George VI.
facts.quote: A design was finalized and construction began in 1938, with Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother, consort of King George VI laying the cornerstone in May 1939.

facts.fact: The building was completed in 1941 but used for the war effort; the Court moved in in January 1946.
facts.quote: The new building was completed in 1941, but was used by government staff for the war effort. Finally, in January 1946, the Supreme Court of Canada moved into the new building.

facts.fact: Ernest Cormier's design is Art Deco, with fluted metal lamp standards at the entrance and a marble lobby, under a châteauesque roof.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Ernest Cormier and is known for its Art Deco style—including two candelabrum-style fluted metal lamp standards that flank the entrance and the marble walls and floors of the lobby—contrasting with the châteauesque roof.

facts.fact: In 2000 the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada named it one of the top 500 buildings produced in Canada in the last millennium.
facts.quote: In 2000, the edifice was named by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada as one of the top 500 buildings produced in Canada during the last millennium.

facts.fact: The nearby Library and Archives Canada Building (1967) was clad in Canadian granite to harmonise with it.
facts.quote: Additionally, the nearby Library and Archives Canada Building completed in 1967 was designed with Canadian granite exterior to harmonize with the Supreme Court of Canada Building.

facts.fact: The Singapore Flyer is an observation wheel in Singapore's Downtown Core, officially opened on 15 April 2008, with 28 air-conditioned capsules of 28 passengers each and a three-storey terminal building.
facts.quote: The Singapore Flyer is an observation wheel at the Downtown Core district of Singapore. Officially opened on 15 April 2008, it has 28 air-conditioned capsules, each able to accommodate 28 passengers, and incorporates a three-story terminal building.

facts.fact: At 165 metres overall, it was the world's tallest Ferris wheel when completed.
facts.quote: The Flyer has an overall height of 165 metres (541 ft), making it the world's tallest Ferris wheel upon completion.

facts.fact: Takenaka and Mitsubishi were the main contractors and Arup the structural engineer.
facts.quote: Takenaka and Mitsubishi were selected as the main contractors, and Arup as the structural engineer.

facts.fact: The development covers about 16,000 m² of floor area on a 33,700 m² site along the Marina Promenade, and one full turn of the wheel takes about 32 minutes.
facts.quote: The development has a gross building area of approximately 16,000 m2 (172,000 sq ft), built on a 33,700 m2 (362,700 sq ft) site along the Marina Promenade. Designed by Arup and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries with a capacity of up to 7.3 million passengers a year, the normally constant rotation of the wheel means that a complete trip lasts approximately 32 minutes.

facts.fact: The capsules are mounted outside the rim, giving continuously unobstructed views.
facts.quote: The Flyer's 28 air-conditioned capsules are mounted outboard of the rim of the wheel structure, providing continuously unobstructed views.

facts.fact: The spindle was fitted in December 2006 and the outer rim completed in April 2007.
facts.quote: The spindle was fitted on 13 December 2006, and the outer rim was completed on 9 April 2007.

facts.fact: On 4 August 2008 the wheel's direction of rotation was reversed on the advice of feng shui masters.
facts.quote: The wheel initially rotated in an anti-clockwise direction when viewed from Marina Centre, but on 4 August 2008 the rotation was reversed on the advice of Feng shui masters.

facts.fact: 8 House is a large mixed-use development in the shape of a figure 8 on the southern edge of Ørestad, Copenhagen.
facts.quote: 8 House (Danish: 8TALLET), also known as Big House, is a large mixed-use development built in the shape of a figure 8 on the southern perimeter of the new suburb of Ørestad in Copenhagen, Denmark.

facts.fact: Designed by Bjarke Ingels of BIG, it holds 61,000 m² of three types of housing and 10,000 m² of shops and offices.
facts.quote: Designed by Bjarke Ingels, founding partner of the Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG), the bow-shaped building consists of 61,000 square metres of three different types of residential housing and 10,000 square metres of retail premises and offices.

facts.fact: The layers of the neighbourhood are stacked and linked by a promenade and cycle track that rise to the 10th floor.
facts.quote: This is achieved by stacking the various ingredients of an urban neighbourhood into layers. They are connected by a promenade and a cycle track which reach up to the 10th floor, allowing businesses and housing to co-exist.

facts.fact: Apartments sit at the top and the commercial programme at the base.
facts.quote: The apartments are placed at the top while the commercial programme unfolds at the base of the building.

facts.fact: The building is lifted at the northeast corner and pushed down at the southwest, letting light and air into the southern courtyard.
facts.quote: This is emphasised by the shape of 8 House which is literally hoisted up in the northeast corner and pushed down at the southwest corner, allowing light and air to enter the southern courtyard.

facts.fact: It began as a perimeter block, squeezed in the middle into a bowtie with two courtyards, joined by a 10-metre-wide passage at the centre.
facts.quote: The scheme was based on the typology of a perimeter block but was squeezed in the middle to form a bowtie shape with two courtyards. At the centre, there is a 10-metre-wide passage connecting the surrounding spaces, the park area to the west and the channel area to the east.

facts.fact: The ramp looping around the complex is meant to encourage interaction between neighbours.
facts.quote: The unusual ramp looping around the complex is designed to foster a sense of community, encouraging interaction between neighbours.

facts.fact: It was Housing Building of the Year at the 2011 World Architecture Festival and won a 2012 AIA Honor Award.
facts.quote:
Housing Building of the Year at the 2011 World Architecture Festival.
The 2012 American Institute of Architects Honor Award for Architecture that recognises achievements that elevate the general quality of the architectural practice.

facts.fact: The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain, and the only well-preserved palace from the medieval Islamic world.
facts.quote: It is one of the most famous monuments of Islamic architecture and the only well-preserved palace from the medieval Islamic world.

facts.fact: It was begun in 1238 by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, first Nasrid emir of Granada, on the Sabika hill.
facts.quote: The building of the complex was begun in 1238 CE by Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, the first Nasrid emir and founder of the Emirate of Granada, the last Muslim state of al-Andalus. It was built on Sabika hill, an outcrop of the Sierra Nevada which had been the site of earlier fortresses and of the 11th-century palace of Samuel ibn Naghrillah.

facts.fact: The main building campaigns, which shaped the royal palaces, came in the 14th century under Yusuf I and Muhammad V.
facts.quote: The most significant construction campaigns, which gave the royal palaces much of their defining character, took place in the 14th century during the reigns of Yusuf I and Muhammad V.

facts.fact: In 1526 Charles V commissioned a Renaissance palace set directly against the Nasrid palaces.
facts.quote: In 1526, Charles V commissioned a new Renaissance-style palace in direct juxtaposition with the Nasrid palaces.

facts.fact: Under the Nasrids it was a self-contained city above Granada, with a mosque, baths, houses, workshops and a water supply system.
facts.quote: During the Nasrid era, the Alhambra was a self-contained city separate from the rest of Granada below. It contained most of the amenities of a Muslim city such as a Friday mosque, hammams (public baths), roads, houses, artisan workshops, a tannery, and a sophisticated water supply system.

facts.fact: The palaces are organised around courtyards, usually with a pool or fountain at the centre.
facts.quote: It is characterized by the use of the courtyard as a central space and basic unit around which other halls and rooms were organized. Courtyards typically had water features at their centre, such as a reflective pool or a fountain.

facts.fact: Decoration is inside: tile mosaics on lower walls, carved stucco above, and muqarnas for vaulted ceilings.
facts.quote: Decoration was focused on the inside of the building and was executed primarily with tile mosaics on lower walls and carved stucco on the upper walls. Geometric patterns, vegetal motifs, and Arabic inscriptions were the main types of decorative motifs. Additionally, "stalactite"-like sculpting, known as muqarnas, was used for three-dimensional features like vaulted ceilings.

facts.fact: The name means 'the red one', from the reddish rammed-earth walls.
facts.quote: The reference to the colour "red" in the name is due to the reddish colour of its walls, which were constructed of rammed earth.

facts.fact: It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
facts.quote: It is now one of Spain's major tourist attractions and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: The Bibliotheca Alexandrina is a major library and cultural centre on the Mediterranean shore in Alexandria, commemorating the ancient Library of Alexandria.
facts.quote: The Bibliotheca Alexandrina (Latin, 'Library of Alexandria'; Egyptian Arabic: مكتبة الإسكندريه, romanized: Maktabat al-’Iskandariyya, Egyptian Arabic pronunciation: [mækˈtæb(e)t eskendeˈɾejjæ]) (BA) is a major library and cultural center on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea in Alexandria, Egypt. It is a commemoration of the Library of Alexandria, once one of the largest libraries worldwide, which was lost in antiquity.

facts.fact: Snøhetta won the 1988 UNESCO design competition among 524 other entries.
facts.quote: UNESCO organized an architectural design competition in 1988 to choose the design. The competition was won by Snøhetta, a Norwegian architectural office, among 524 other entries.

facts.fact: Construction began in 1995 and the complex was inaugurated on 16 October 2002.
facts.quote: Construction work began in 1995, and, after some additional US$220 million had been spent, the complex was officially inaugurated on 16 October 2002.

facts.fact: The main reading room covers 20,000 m² on eleven cascading levels and was the largest in the world when built.
facts.quote: The library has shelf space for eight million books, with the main reading room covering 20,000 square metres (220,000 sq ft) on eleven cascading levels. At the time of construction, the reading room was the largest in the world.

facts.fact: The reading room sits under a 32-metre-high glass-panelled roof about 160 m across, tilted toward the sea like a sundial.
facts.quote: The main reading room stands beneath a 32-meter-high glass-panelled roof, tilted out toward the sea like a sundial, and measuring some 160 m in diameter.

facts.fact: Its grey granite walls are carved with characters from 120 scripts, designed by Norwegian artist Jorunn Sannes.
facts.quote: The walls are of gray granite, carved with characters from 120 scripts. The characters carved into the granite wall were designed by Norwegian artist Jorunn Sannes, as part of the Snøhetta design team.

facts.fact: The complex also holds a conference centre, specialised libraries, museums, galleries, a planetarium and a manuscript restoration laboratory.
facts.quote: The complex also houses a conference center, several specialized libraries, multiple museums and art galleries, a planetarium, and a manuscript restoration laboratory.

facts.fact: The site was chosen in 1974, close to where the ancient library once stood.
facts.quote: The idea of reviving the Library of Alexandria dates back to 1974, when a committee set up by Alexandria University selected a plot of land for its new library between the campus and the seafront, close to where the ancient library once stood.

facts.fact: The Bank of China Tower is a skyscraper at 1 Garden Road in Central, Hong Kong, headquarters of the Bank of China (Hong Kong).
facts.quote: The Bank of China Tower (BOC Tower) is a skyscraper located in Central, Hong Kong. Located at 1 Garden Road on Hong Kong Island, the tower houses the headquarters of the Bank of China (Hong Kong) Limited.

facts.fact: It is known for its triangular frameworks covered by glass curtain walls.
facts.quote: One of the most recognisable landmarks in Hong Kong, the building is notable for its distinct shape and design, consisting of triangular frameworks covered by glass curtain walls.

facts.fact: It was designed by I. M. Pei and L. C. Pei of I. M. Pei and Partners.
facts.quote: The building was designed by Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei and L. C. Pei of I. M. Pei and Partners.

facts.fact: It was the tallest building in Hong Kong and Asia from 1990 to 1992 and the first supertall skyscraper outside the United States.
facts.quote: It was the tallest building in Hong Kong and Asia from 1990 to 1992, and it was the first supertall skyscraper outside the United States, the first to break the 305 m (1,000 ft) mark.

facts.fact: The 72-storey tower is 315 m high, or 367.4 m with its two masts.
facts.quote: Designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect I. M. Pei, the building is 315.0 m (1,033.5 ft) high with two masts reaching 367.4 m (1,205.4 ft) high. The 72-storey building is located near Central MTR station.

facts.fact: Four steel columns at the corners carry the whole structure, with the triangular frameworks transferring the weight onto them.
facts.quote: The whole structure is supported by the four steel columns at the corners of the building, with the triangular frameworks transferring the weight of the structure onto these four columns.

facts.fact: Leslie E. Robertson, engineer of the original World Trade Center towers, did the structural design.
facts.quote: Structural engineer Leslie E. Robertson, best known for his work on the Twin Towers of the original World Trade Center, provided the structural engineering design, while Jaros, Baum & Bolles was the mechanical, electrical and plumbing engineer.

facts.fact: Feng shui practitioners criticised its sharp edges and many 'X' shapes, and Pei modified the design somewhat before construction.
facts.quote: The building has been criticised by some practitioners of feng shui for its sharp edges and its negative symbolism by the numerous 'X' shapes in its original design, though Pei modified the design to some degree before construction following this feedback.

facts.fact: The Virgilio Barco Library is a public library in western Bogotá, part of the city's BibloRed network.
facts.quote: Virgilio Barco Public Library is a Public library in the western sector of Bogotá, Colombia. It is a part of BibloRed, the District's Public Library Network.

facts.fact: It was designed by Rogelio Salmona and forms part of the Simón Bolívar Metropolitan Park.
facts.quote: The building was designed by architect Rogelio Salmona, and forms part of the Simón Bolívar Metropolitan Park.

facts.fact: It opened on 21 December 2001 and is named after former President Virgilio Barco Vargas.
facts.quote: Its inauguration took place on 21 December 2001, named after former President Virgilio Barco Vargas.

facts.fact: The design is notable for its water management, with pools outside the building.
facts.quote: The design of the building is notable for its emphasis of water management, with water pools on the outside.

facts.fact: With its park, it is one of seven sites in the serial property 'The architectural legacy of Rogelio Salmona', put on Colombia's World Heritage Tentative List in 2022.
facts.quote: The library and its surrounding park together form one of seven sites which make up the serial property "The architectural legacy of Rogelio Salmona: an ethical, political, social and poetic manifesto." Colombia's permanent delegation to UNESCO submitted the site to the country's Tentative List for the World Heritage List in 2022.

facts.fact: Salmona designed the library around its relationship with the surrounding public space.
facts.quote: For the construction of the library, Salmona took into account its interrelation with the public space, forming a series of geographical, landscape, historical, and experiential values.

facts.fact: The Calgary Central Library is the flagship of Calgary Public Library, in the East Village, opened on 1 November 2018.
facts.quote: The Calgary Central Library, also known as the Calgary New Central Library (NCL), is a public library in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, and the flagship branch of the Calgary Public Library system. The building is located in the Downtown East Village neighbourhood and opened on November 1, 2018, replacing an earlier central branch built in the 1960s in Downtown Calgary.

facts.fact: The four-storey building cost CA$245 million and was designed by Snøhetta and DIALOG, who won a design competition in 2013.
facts.quote: The four-storey building cost CA$245 million to construct and was designed by American-Norwegian architecture firm Snøhetta and Canadian firm DIALOG after the two firms' joint bid won a design competition in 2013.

facts.fact: The oval building is raised one floor above the street to bridge a CTrain light rail tunnel and an open plaza linking the East Village to Downtown.
facts.quote: The entire building is oval-shaped and is elevated one floor above street level to cover a CTrain light rail tunnel and an open plaza, included with the intention of connecting Calgary's East Village to Downtown.

facts.fact: The entrance is framed by wood-clad arches inspired by the arched clouds of Alberta's Chinook winds.
facts.quote: The entrance is framed by wood-clad arches inspired by the shape of arched clouds made by Chinook winds in Alberta.

facts.fact: The textured façade uses translucent fritted glass to screen private study areas and clear glass where public areas can be seen from outside.
facts.quote: The exterior of the Calgary Central Library is wrapped in a textured façade, with translucent fritted glass panels used to shield private study areas and clear glass to make public areas viewable from the outside.

facts.fact: The 22,000 m² interior centres on a four-storey atrium under a skylight.
facts.quote: The 22,000-square-metre (240,000 sq ft) interior is centered around a four-storey central atrium topped by a skylight.

facts.fact: Sustainable features include triple-pane windows and low-VOC finishes.
facts.quote: The library features several sustainable design features, such as triple-pane windows to save energy on climate control and finishings made of low volatile organic compound materials.

facts.fact: Construction began by encasing a 135-metre section of the Red Line light rail, from May 2014 to September 2015.
facts.quote: The first stage of construction was the $25 million encapsulation of a 135-metre (443 ft) section of light rail used by Calgary Transit's Red Line, which emerges from a tunnel under the site. The light rail encapsulation began in May 2014 and was completed in September 2015, allowing for construction of the above ground portion of the Central Library to begin.

facts.fact: Dipoli is on Aalto University's Otaniemi campus in Espoo, designed by Reima and Raili Pietilä and opened in 1966.
facts.quote: Dipoli is a building located in the Aalto University's Otaniemi campus in Espoo in Otakaari 24, Finland. It was designed by architects Reima and Raili Pietilä and opened in 1966.

facts.fact: It was built as the Student Union building of Helsinki University of Technology after a 1961 competition.
facts.quote: In 1961 an architecture competition was held to decide what would become the new building for the Student Union of the university.

facts.fact: Because of the rocky site and demands for adaptability, no first prize was given; the Pietiläs' design was finally chosen.
facts.quote: Due to the challenging rocky location and adaptability requirements none of the competition entries fulfilled all the jury's demands and the first prize was not awarded: the second prize was shared by the architect couple Reima and Raili Pietilä and Osmo Lappo, who were asked to further develop their proposals. Finally, the design by the Pietiläs was chosen as the basis for the new building.

facts.fact: It uses materials from Finnish nature such as pine, copper and natural rock, and has 500 windows, only four of them identical.
facts.quote: The building uses extensively materials from Finnish nature, such as pine wood, copper, and natural rocks. Dipoli has 500 windows, of which only four are identical.

facts.fact: The building is seen as a key example of organic architecture.
facts.quote: The building is seen as a key example of organic architecture.

facts.fact: Its name is a pun: 'dipole' in Finnish, and also 'the second Poly' of the polytechnic students.
facts.quote: The name of the building is a pun: it can mean dipole in Finnish, but also "the second Poly", the second building of the polytechnic students.

facts.fact: It was renovated in 2015–2017 and became the university's main building.
facts.quote: The building was extensively renovated between 2015 and 2017, turning it into the new main building for the university.

facts.fact: The METI Handmade School is a primary school for 168 students in Rudrapur, Bangladesh, built with local craftsmen mainly from mud and bamboo.
facts.quote: The METI Handmade School, a primary school for 168 students located in Rudrapur in Dinajpur district of Bangladesh, was built with the assistance of local craftsmen making use of traditional materials, primarily mud and bamboo.

facts.fact: Anna Heringer designed it with Eike Roswag, using regional methods and local materials with new approaches for efficiency and structural integrity.
facts.quote: Anna Heringer worked together with her colleague Eike Roswag, developing a design based on regional construction methods and local materials but introducing new approaches for efficiency and structural integrity.

facts.fact: Improved bamboo structure and lashing made a second floor possible, and brick foundations protect the earth walls from moisture.
facts.quote: As a result of improvements to the bamboo structures and lashing, it was possible to add a second floor to the building. Brick foundations were used to minimize the effects of moisture on the earthen walls.

facts.fact: Ground-floor classrooms have mud walls; upper-floor rooms have slatted bamboo walls giving diffused light and natural ventilation.
facts.quote: The classrooms on the ground floor are enclosed by a mud wall while those on the first floor have slatted bamboo walls providing diffused light and natural ventilation.

facts.fact: Advances included a damp-proof course and straw added to the earth mix.
facts.quote: Among the notable advances made in the use of local materials were the introduction of a damp proof course and a brick foundation as well as the addition of straw to the loam mixture of earth and water.

facts.fact: It was built in four months, from September to December 2005.
facts.quote: The construction was completed over a period of four months from September 2005 to December 2005.

facts.fact: It received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2007.
facts.quote: An example of sustainable architecture, the project received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2007 for its simple, humane approach and beauty, and for the level of cooperation achieved between architects, craftsmen, clients and users.

facts.fact: The Auditorio de Tenerife is an auditorium by Santiago Calatrava beside the Atlantic in Santa Cruz de Tenerife.
facts.quote: Designed by architect Santiago Calatrava, it is located on the Avenue of the Constitution in the Canarian capital, and next to the Atlantic Ocean in the southern part of Port of Santa Cruz de Tenerife.

facts.fact: Construction ran from 1997 to 2003, and it was inaugurated on 26 September 2003.
facts.quote: Construction began in 1997 and was completed in 2003. The auditorium was inaugurated on 26 September of that year in the presence of Felipe, Prince of Asturias, and was later visited by former U.S. President Bill Clinton.

facts.fact: Much of the surface is white trencadís, with coloured trencadís on the plaza's retaining walls.
facts.quote: Much of the surface is covered with white trencadís, while colorful trencadís is used as decorative elements in the retaining walls of the plaza on which the building stands.

facts.fact: The domed Symphony Hall seats 1,616 in an amphitheatre.
facts.quote: The main hall or Symphony, crowned by a dome, has 1,616 seats in an amphitheater.

facts.fact: The chamber hall, with 422 seats, repeats the symphony hall's amphitheatre at a smaller scale.
facts.quote: The chamber hall, with 422 seats, reproduces the symphony hall amphitheater on a smaller scale.

facts.fact: Its great arched roof, 15–20 cm thick, rests on only two points, its tip seeming to hang in the air.
facts.quote: The arched roof varies in thickness from 15-20cm. It is the only large arch supported by only two points, while the tip appears to be suspended, defying gravity.

facts.fact: It is home to the Tenerife Symphony Orchestra.
facts.quote: It is one of the major attractions of Tenerife and home to the Orquesta Sinfónica de Tenerife (Tenerife Symphony Orchestra).

facts.fact: Its trencadís tiles are damaged and the inside has moisture problems.
facts.quote: There is visible damage to the trencadís tiles and the inside has moisture problems.

facts.fact: The Danish Jewish Museum sits inside the Royal Library's old Galley House in Copenhagen.
facts.quote: The Danish Jewish Museum (Danish: Dansk Jødisk Museum), in Copenhagen, Denmark, sits inside the Danish Royal Library’s old Galley House and exhibits Danish Jewish historical artifacts and art.

facts.fact: Designed by Daniel Libeskind, it remembers the Danish Jews saved from Nazi persecution by fellow Danes in October 1943; it opened in June 2004.
facts.quote: Designed by architect Daniel Libeskind, the building memorializes the story of Danish Jews who were saved from Nazi persecution by their fellow Danes in October 1943. Construction of the Museum began in March 2003 and the museum opened in June 2004.

facts.fact: The boat house it occupies was built by King Christian IV around 1600.
facts.quote: At the turn of the seventeenth century, King Christian IV built Denmark's Royal Boat House, which was later renovated in 1906, during the construction of the adjacent Royal Library.

facts.fact: It is Denmark's first official museum dedicated to a minority or immigrant group.
facts.quote: The   Museum  is the first official museum in Denmark dedicated to a minority or immigrant group.

facts.fact: The building is organised as a series of planes that carve fractured corridors and slanted floors.
facts.quote: The whole building is organized as a series of planes, each corresponding to a particular field of religious discourse. Together, the planes, named Exodus, Wilderness, The Giving of the Law, and The Promised Land, carve interior corridors of fractured passageways and slanted floors.

facts.fact: The winding exhibition corridors form the letters of the Hebrew word Mitzvah, 'good deed'.
facts.quote: These corridors comprise the museum's exhibition spaces and, as they wind, they form the letters for the Hebrew word Mitzvah, meaning “good deed.”

facts.fact: It won the American Architect Award in 2005.
facts.quote: American Architect Award, 2005

facts.fact: Ristinkirkko, the Church of the Cross, is the main church of Lahti, completed in 1978 as one of Alvar Aalto's last designs.
facts.quote: Ristinkirkko (English: Church of the Cross) is the main church in Lahti, Finland. The modernist church, completed in 1978, was one of the last design projects of the renowned Finnish architect Alvar Aalto.

facts.fact: Aalto died in May 1976 and never saw it finished; Elissa Aalto oversaw the final stages.
facts.quote: He died in May 1976, whereas the church was only completed two years later, consecrated during the Advent season of 1978. The final stages of the project were instead overseen by Aalto's wife, architect Elissa Aalto.

facts.fact: The exterior is mostly red brick, with a massive cast-concrete belfry rising 40 metres.
facts.quote: The exterior of the church building is constructed mostly of red brick, with a massive cast concrete belfry rising from its roof to a height of 40 metres (130 ft) above the surrounding terrain.

facts.fact: The interior is light, with white walls and large windows.
facts.quote: In contrast, the interior is light, with white walls and large windows providing natural daylight.

facts.fact: The plan is an equilateral triangle with two points cut off, forming an irregular pentagon.
facts.quote: The basic shape of the overall floorplan is an equilateral triangle, with two of the three points cut off, forming an irregular pentagon.

facts.fact: The nave narrows toward the chancel under a fan-shaped ceiling that steps down, like a theatre or concert hall.
facts.quote: Viewed from the main entrance, the nave of the church narrows towards the chancel, located in one of the northern corner of the triangle, and the fan-shaped ceiling becomes gradually lower, creating an impression of a theatre or concert hall.

facts.fact: The south front facing the market square has 52 small windows forming a large cross.
facts.quote: The southerly elevation, with the main entrance facing towards the city's central market square, is dominated by a pattern of 52 small windows, forming the shape of a large cross.

facts.fact: Aalto won the design competition in 1950, but controversy delayed the commission until 1969.
facts.quote: In 1950, an architectural design contest was held for a new church, and was won by Aalto. However, the plan to demolish the old church and build a new modernist one sparked off a heated controversy which lasted almost two decades, and it wasn't until 1969 that the Lahti Parish had received green light and were in a position to commission a full architectural plan from Aalto.

facts.fact: 21_21 Design Sight is a design museum in Roppongi, Tokyo, opened in 2007.
facts.quote: 21_21 Design Sight is a museum in Roppongi in Minato, Tokyo, Japan, which opened in 2007.

facts.fact: It was created by architect Tadao Ando and fashion designer Issey Miyake.
facts.quote: The museum, a design museum, was created by architect Tadao Ando and fashion designer Issey Miyake.

facts.fact: Ando meant it as a place for researching design, not only for showing exhibits.
facts.quote: "The idea was to create not only a museum that shows exhibits," says Ando, "but also a place for researching the potentiality of design as an element that enriches our daily life, a place that fosters the public's interest in design by arousing in them different sights and perspectives on how we can view the world and the objects surrounding us."

facts.fact: Ando's building sits on the edge of the park, with 1,700 m² including two galleries and a café.
facts.quote: The building, designed by Ando, is on the edge of the park area, and features 1,700 square meters (18,300 sq ft) of floor space, including two galleries and an attached cafe run by chef and restaurateur Takamasa Uetake.

facts.fact: The split-level concrete structure has a steel roof inspired by Miyake's A-POC ('A Piece of Cloth') and 14-metre glass panels.
facts.quote: The split-level concrete structure includes a hand-sanded steel roof (whose design was inspired by Issey Miyake's A-POC ("A Piece of Cloth") concept) and 14-meter (46 ft) long glass panels.

facts.fact: It is a Roman Catholic church on Jiřího z Poděbrad Square in Prague's Vinohrady, built 1929–1932 to a design by Jože Plečnik.
facts.quote: The Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord (Czech: Kostel Nejsvětějšího Srdce Páně) is a Roman Catholic church at Jiřího z Poděbrad Square in Prague's Vinohrady district. It was built between 1929 and 1932 and designed by the Slovene architect Jože Plečnik.

facts.fact: Plečnik drew on early Christian and ancient patterns.
facts.quote: Plečnik found the inspiration for this construction in old Christian and ancient patterns.

facts.fact: It was one of three projects in Prague marking the 1000th anniversary of St Wenceslas's death.
facts.quote: This was one of three new buildings constructed in 1929 in Prague, inspired by the 1000th anniversary of the death of St. Wenceslas.

facts.fact: It is considered one of the most significant Czech religious buildings of the 20th century.
facts.quote: It is considered one of the most significant Czech religious constructions of the 20th century.

facts.fact: Its broad 42-metre tower wall holds a glazed clock 7.6 m across, the largest in the Czech Republic.
facts.quote: In the wide 42 m high tower wall is a huge, 7.6 m diameter glazed clock (the largest in the Czech Republic).

facts.fact: The basement holds a spacious chapel with a wooden coffered ceiling.
facts.quote: In the basement is a spacious chapel with a wooden caisson ceiling.

facts.fact: It has been a national cultural monument since 2010.
facts.quote: Since 2010, the church has been ranked among national cultural monuments.

facts.fact: It was Plečnik's final work in Prague.
facts.quote: His final work in Prague was the Church of the Most Sacred Heart of Our Lord (Roman Catholic, 1929–32).

facts.fact: Al-Azhar Park is a public park in al-Darb al-Ahmar, Historic Cairo.
facts.quote: Al-Azhar Park (Arabic: حديقة الأزهر, romanized: Ḥadīqat al-Azhar) is a public park located in qism al-Darb al-Ahmar, in Historic Cairo, Egypt.

facts.fact: It was created by the Historic Cities Support Programme of the Aga Khan Trust for Culture.
facts.quote: The park was created by the Historic Cities Support Programme of the Aga Khan Trust for Culture (AKTC), an entity of the Aga Khan Development Network.

facts.fact: The site had long been a landfill, with debris up to 40 metres deep in places by the late 20th century.
facts.quote: The site was historically used as a landfill, particularly for debris from redevelopment. The practice intensified in the 16th century during the Mamluk Sultanate. By the late-20th century, the fill was 40 metres (130 ft) deep in some parts.

facts.fact: Over one million cubic metres of fill were removed.
facts.quote: Over one million cubic meters of fill were removed.

facts.fact: Three water tanks for Cairo's drinking water were added midway, and the design was revised to integrate them.
facts.quote: While the designers grappled with the technical difficulties at hand posed by the terrain and soil the government introduces an additional unexpected constraint at halfway through the process: three cisterns were to be integrated into the terrain to improve the supply of potable water to the city of Cairo. Works had to be interrupted and the design revised to integrate the new three elements.

facts.fact: Opened in 2005, its gardens recall historic Islamic gardens, mixing modern and traditional elements.
facts.quote: Opened to the public in 2005, the gardens of al-Azhar are reminiscent of historical Islamic gardens, with a blend of modern and traditional elements.

facts.fact: Terraced formal gardens, fountains, Mamluk multicoloured stonework, sunken gardens, intersecting waterways and Islamic geometry are set in a contemporary design.
facts.quote: The central terraced formal gardens, emphatic use of fountains, Mamluk multicolored stonework, sunken gardens, intersecting waterways and bold Islamic geometry are all integrated into a contemporary site design; cafes are situated at the entrance, playgrounds and scenic overlooks are arranged along curving paths.

facts.fact: Excavation uncovered a 1.5-kilometre section of the historic Ayyubid wall, up to 15 metres deep.
facts.quote: While the excavation was still ongoing, under the mounts of garbage a treasure was uncovered: a wall to a depth of 15 meters and a 1.5 kilometers section. The forgotten historic Ayyubid wall and towers were revealed in their entire splendor.

facts.fact: Deutsche Bank Place is a 240-metre, 39-storey skyscraper in Sydney.
facts.quote: Deutsche Bank Place is a 240-metre-high (790 ft), 39-storey skyscraper in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia.

facts.fact: It stands at 126 Phillip Street, at the corner of Hunter Street, across the road from Chifley Tower.
facts.quote: It is located at 126 Phillip Street (corner of Hunter Street) in the north-eastern end of the central business district, across the road from Chifley Tower.

facts.fact: It was built from 2002 to 2005 to a design by Norman Foster of Foster + Partners.
facts.quote: Construction began in 2002 and was completed in 2005. The building's architect is Norman Foster of Foster + Partners.

facts.fact: Deutsche Bank is the main tenant, occupying seven floors and holding the naming rights.
facts.quote: Deutsche Bank is the primary tenant, occupying seven floors and owning the naming rights.

facts.fact: The Atatürk Cultural Center (AKM) is a concert hall, theatre and cultural centre along the east side of Taksim Square, Istanbul.
facts.quote: The Atatürk Cultural Center (Turkish: Atatürk Kültür Merkezi), commonly called the AKM, is a concert hall, theatre and cultural centre running along the eastern side of Taksim Square in Beyoğlu, Istanbul.

facts.fact: The original opened in 1969, closed in 2008, was demolished in 2018 and rebuilt in 2021, reopening on 29 October 2021.
facts.quote: Originally opened on April 12, 1969, it was closed for renovation works in 2008, but was ultimately demolished in 2018 and rebuilt in 2021 as a state-of-the-art cultural complex. On October 29, 2021, it reopened to the public after a 13-year interval.

facts.fact: The new AKM was designed by Murat Tabanlıoğlu, son of Hayati Tabanlıoğlu, architect of the original; Werner Sobek engineered a transparent façade opening onto Taksim Square.
facts.quote: The new AKM building was designed by Murat Tabanlıoğlu, the son of Hayati Tabanlıoğlu who had designed the original AKM building. Werner Sobek AG was responsible for the facade engineering, creating a transparent facade that opens the building to Taksim Square.

facts.fact: The new centre has five sections totalling 95,000 m².
facts.quote: The new Cultural Center consists of five sections, with a total area of 95,000 m2 (1,020,000 sq ft).

facts.fact: It holds a theatre, cinema, concert halls, exhibition and convention halls, a library, a museum and an art gallery.
facts.quote: It features a theatre, cinema, concert halls, an exhibition center, a convention hall, Vitali Hakko Creative Industries Library, a museum, an art gallery, a Paşabahçe art glass store, cafés, and restaurants.

facts.fact: Construction of the new complex began on 10 February 2019.
facts.quote: On 10 February 2019, construction of the new complex began with a groundbreaking ceremony attended by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

facts.fact: The original building, first called the Istanbul Culture Palace, opened on 12 April 1969, 23 years after it was first proposed.
facts.quote: The building, originally called the Istanbul Culture Palace, was completed in 13 years and opened on April 12, 1969, twenty-three years after the initial proposal.

facts.fact: Renzo Piano designed the Parco della Musica, a complex of music performance halls in Rome, from 1994 to 2002.
facts.quote: His other projects begun in the 1990s included the New Metropolis Museum in Amsterdam, which later became the science museum and technology NEMO (1992–1997), placed on the edge of the harbor, and resembling the hull of an enormous ship; the Parco della Musica, a complex of music performance halls in Rome (1994–2002), Each was entirely different from the others, and in this period it was difficult to discern a specific element that or style defined his architecture, other than careful craftsmanship and attention to detail.

facts.fact: It stands in the Rome neighbourhood that hosted the 1960 Summer Olympics.
facts.quote: The Parco della Musica is the complex of music venues located in the Rome neighborhood which hosted the 1960 Summer Olympics.

facts.fact: It has three halls; the largest seats 2,800 and was Europe's largest symphonic concert hall when completed.
facts.quote: The park has three theaters, the largest with 2800 seats; when completed it was the largest symphonic concert hall in Europe.

facts.fact: Piano took the vineyard-style seating around the orchestra of the Berlin Philharmonic as his model for the interior.
facts.quote: Piano acknowledged that his inspiration for the interior plan was the vineyard style seating, placed around the orchestra, of the Berlin Philharmonic by Hans Sharon.

facts.fact: The three brick halls are covered in steel shells that a New York Times critic likened to armadillos, with interiors heavy with wood and fabric.
facts.quote: The three brick concert halls covered with what New York Times critic Sam Lubell described as  "weathered armadillo-like steel shells,"  which looked forbidding in photographs but in person were "lovely"; and noted that the theaters "inside are heavy with wood, fabrics, and typical Piano elegance."

facts.fact: Al Hamra Tower is the tallest building in Kuwait, built from 2005 to 2011.
facts.quote: The Al Hamra Tower is a skyscraper in Kuwait City, Kuwait. It is the tallest building in Kuwait. Construction of the skyscraper started in 2005. It was completed in 2011.

facts.fact: Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill with Ramshir and Callison, it is the world's tallest curved concrete skyscraper, at 414 m.
facts.quote: Designed by architectural firms Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and Ramshir and Callison, it is the tallest curved concrete skyscraper in the world, and the 40th tallest building in the world at 414 m (1,358 ft).

facts.fact: Glass wraps the east, north and west sides, limiting reflective surface on the south façade, which is faced in brushed Jura limestone.
facts.quote: The building utilizes wrapped glass on the east, north, and west both for aesthetics and to reduce the amount of reflective surface area on the south facade, which also features brushed Jura limestone.

facts.fact: Flared walls from the core's southwest and southeast corners run the full height, and the lobby is a column-free 24 metres tall.
facts.quote: Flared walls reaching from the southwest and southeast corners of the core span the entire height of the tower, and there is a column-free 24-meter-tall lobby.

facts.fact: Time magazine listed it among the best inventions of 2011.
facts.quote: The tower was included in the list of the best inventions of 2011 by Time magazine.

facts.fact: It won the 2011 Emporis Skyscraper Award.
facts.quote: 2011: Emporis Skyscraper Award

facts.fact: 4 World Trade Center is a skyscraper on Greenwich Street at the southeast corner of the World Trade Center site, designed by Fumihiko Maki and 978 ft (298 m) tall.
facts.quote: The tower is located on Greenwich Street at the southeastern corner of the World Trade Center site. Fumihiko Maki designed the 978 ft-tall (298 m) building.

facts.fact: Ground was broken in January 2008 and it opened on 13 November 2013.
facts.quote: The current building's groundbreaking took place in January 2008, and it opened to tenants and the public on November 13, 2013.

facts.fact: Maki and Associates designed it as a 'minimalist tower with an abstract sculptural presence'.
facts.quote: According to Engineering News-Record, Maki and Associates had designed 4 WTC as a "minimalist tower with an abstract sculptural presence".

facts.fact: Floors 7 to 46 are parallelograms in plan, reflecting the shape of the site; floors 48 to 63 are trapezoids.
facts.quote: Floors 7 to 46 each span 44,000 square feet (4,100 m2) and are parallelogram in plan, reflecting the shape of the World Trade Center site. the shape of a parallelogram. Floors 48 to 63 each cover 36,000 square feet (3,300 m2) and are trapezoidal in plan.

facts.fact: The façade is mostly reflective glass, clear at the lobby.
facts.quote: Most of the facade is made of reflective glass, except at the lobby, where the facade is made of clear glass.

facts.fact: The west façade, facing the 9/11 Memorial, has no louvers; the architects wanted the building to 'pay deference to the memorial'.
facts.quote: The western facade of the tower, which faces the National September 11 Memorial, does not have louvers. The New York Daily News wrote that Maki and Associates wanted the building's design to "pay deference to the memorial".

facts.fact: The two-storey lobby, 46 feet high, faces the 9/11 Memorial.
facts.quote: The building's ground-floor lobby is two stories high, with a 46-foot (14 m) ceiling. The lobby occupies the western part of the ground floor, facing the National September 11 Memorial.

facts.fact: New York magazine called it 'pretty exquisite'.
facts.quote: While it has criticized his 51 Astor Place project as "out of place," New York magazine called Tower 4 "pretty exquisite."

facts.fact: The Federal Palace in Bern houses the Swiss Federal Assembly and the Federal Council.
facts.quote: The Federal Palace is a building in Bern housing the Swiss Federal Assembly (legislature) and the Federal Council (executive).

facts.fact: It is a listed symmetrical complex just over 300 metres long, of national importance.
facts.quote: The building is a listed symmetrical complex just over 300 metres (980 ft) long. It is considered one of the most important historic buildings in the country and listed in the Swiss Inventory of Cultural Assets of National Importance.

facts.fact: Hans Wilhelm Auer built the east wing (1884–1892) and then the central parliament building (1894–1902).
facts.quote: To solve pressing space problems, the east wing ("Bundeshaus Ost") was built from 1884 to 1892 under Hans Wilhelm Auer. Under Auer's direction, the parliament building in the center was erected between 1894 and 1902 to conclude the project.

facts.fact: The parliament building is neo-Renaissance, with a portico and a striking dome, more monumental than the sober administrative wings.
facts.quote: The sobriety of the two wings corresponds to their main purpose as administrative buildings, contrasting with the  more monumental parliament building constructed in neo-Renaissance style with a portico and a striking dome.

facts.fact: Bernese sandstone façades help it blend into Bern's Old City.
facts.quote: Despite its size and dominant position, the Federal Palace blends into the cityscape due to the use of Bernese sandstone for the facades.

facts.fact: About 30 types of stone from 13 cantons were used, so that the building represents the whole country.
facts.quote: No fewer than 30 types of stone from 13 different cantons and half-cantons were used in the construction of the building.

facts.fact: The domed hall is laid out as a Swiss cross and separates the two chambers.
facts.quote: The central assembly building is dominated by a domed hall in the layout of a Swiss cross. It separates the two chambers of the National Council (south) and the Council of States (north).

facts.fact: Auer modelled the free-standing, bridge-like staircase on the Opéra Garnier in Paris.
facts.quote: He designed the staircase as a bridge-like structure standing freely in space, following the example of the Opéra Garnier in Paris.

facts.fact: The Yokohama Museum of Art, founded in 1989, is in Yokohama's Minato Mirai 21 district next to the Landmark Tower.
facts.quote: Yokohama Museum of Art (横浜美術館, Yokohama Bijutsukan), founded in 1989, is located in the futuristic Minato Mirai 21 district of the Japanese city Yokohama, next to the Yokohama Landmark Tower.

facts.fact: The building was designed by Kenzo Tange, winner of the 1987 Pritzker Prize.
facts.quote: The building which houses the Yokohama Museum of Art was designed by Kenzo Tange, the Japanese architect who won the 1987 Pritzker Prize for architecture.

facts.fact: Its main hall is 18 metres tall and open to the second and third floors.
facts.quote: The museum's main hall is 18 meters tall and is open to the second and third floors.

facts.fact: A glass ceiling brings daylight into the hall, controlled by louvres.
facts.quote: A glass ceiling allows natural light into the space. Louvers control the light levels.

facts.fact: The building has been described as airy and well lit.
facts.quote: The structure is described as an "attractive and spacious building " that is "airy and well-lit".

facts.fact: The museum reopened after renovation for the 2023 Yokohama Triennale.
facts.quote: In 2023, the eighth edition of the Triennale will for the first time be held at the renovated Yokohama Museum of Art.

facts.fact: Tadao Ando, who designed the Saka no Ue no Kumo Museum in Matsuyama, also designed the Ryōtarō Shiba Memorial Museum.
facts.quote: The museum was constructed by Tadao Ando. He is also known for the construction of Ryōtarō Shiba Memorial Museum.

facts.fact: The Art Gallery of Ontario is on Dundas Street West in Toronto; at 45,000 m² it is one of the largest art museums in North America.
facts.quote: Located on Dundas Street West in the Grange Park neighbourhood of downtown Toronto, the museum complex takes up 45,000 square metres (480,000 sq ft) of physical space, making it one of the largest art museums in North America and the second-largest art museum in Toronto, after the Royal Ontario Museum.

facts.fact: From 2004 to 2008 Frank Gehry led a CA$276 million redevelopment, with Adamson Associates.
facts.quote: From 2004 to 2008, the museum's building underwent a CA$276 million redevelopment, led by Canadian-born architect Frank Gehry with local associate architect Adamson Associates Architects.

facts.fact: Gehry was asked to expand and revitalise the museum, not design a new one, uniting parts left by six earlier expansions.
facts.quote: Gehry was commissioned to expand and revitalize the museum, not to design a new building; as such, one of the challenges he faced was to unite the disparate areas of the building that had become "a bit of a hodgepodge" after six previous expansions dating back to the 1920s.

facts.fact: The Galleria Italia is a 200-metre glass, steel and wood canopy along Dundas Street, also a viewing hall on the second level.
facts.quote: The Galleria Italia is a 200 m (660 ft) glass, steel, and wood projecting canopy at the fronting of Dundas Street, also acting as a viewing hall on the second level of the building.

facts.fact: About 1,800 glued-laminated timber pieces form the Galleria's façade.
facts.quote: Approximately 1,800 glued laminated timber pieces were used on the facade of the Galleria Italia; and 2,500 timber connectors.

facts.fact: A five-storey South Gallery block was added, clad in glass and titanium panels, with a spiral staircase projecting outside.
facts.quote: The southern portion of the museum building also saw redevelopment, with the construction of a five-storey South Gallery block, and a protruding spiral staircase that connects the fourth and fifth levels of the block. The exterior facade of the South Gallery Block includes glass and custom-made titanium panels, and like the Dundas Street fronting, is supported by glued laminated timber.

facts.fact: Reopened in November 2008, it gained 20% more floor area and 47% more space to view art.
facts.quote: The redeveloped building opened in November 2008, with the transformation increasing the museum's total floor area by 20 percent for a total of 45,000 square metres (480,000 sq ft); as well as increasing the art viewing space by 47%.

facts.fact: The expansion was praised for its restraint; The Globe and Mail called it a 'restrained masterpiece'.
facts.quote: The completed expansion received wide acclaim, notably for the restraint of its design. An editorial in The Globe and Mail called it a "restrained masterpiece", noting: "The proof of Mr. Gehry's genius lies in his deft adaptation to unusual circumstances.

facts.fact: Herz-Jesu-Kirche is a Catholic church in Munich's Neuhausen-Nymphenburg; the current, third church was built 1997–2000 to plans by Allmann Sattler Wappner.
facts.quote: There has been a church on the site since 1890, but the current (and third) church was built between 1997 and 2000 to plans by architects Allmann Sattler Wappner.

facts.fact: After the second church burned down in 1994, a competition drew 158 entries and was won by Allmann Sattler Wappner.
facts.quote: The archdiocese’s call for a new church design resulted in 158 submissions, and the architects Allmann Sattler Wappner won the competition.

facts.fact: The church is a steel-framed glass box 16 m high, 21 m wide and 48 m long.
facts.quote: The church building consists of a rectangular glass box which is 16 metres (52 ft) high, 21 metres (69 ft) wide, and 48 metres (157 ft) long. The glass structure is supported by a steel frame.

facts.fact: Its glass front can open fully as a pair of double-winged doors, reportedly the largest church doors in the world.
facts.quote: On special occasions, the front of the glass box can be fully opened as a pair of double-winged doors, reportedly forming the largest set of church doors in the world.

facts.fact: Inside the glass box stands a second, wooden box that forms the worship space.
facts.quote: Within the glass structure stands a second, wooden box that forms the main worship space.

facts.fact: The glass walls go from transparent at the front to opaque near the altar.
facts.quote: The outer glass walls vary from transparent at the front to opaque near the altar.

facts.fact: The inner walls are slatted maple and oak, opening up toward the altar, so daylight filters through and changes with the sun.
facts.quote: The inner wooden walls are made of slatted maple and oak panels, and the angle at which the slats are positioned also varies from front to back, becoming more open as they approach the altar. Natural light enters through the slats, with its intensity varying according to the position of the sun.

facts.fact: A free-standing metal campanile, 37 metres tall, stands at the street side of the square.
facts.quote: The free-standing campanile stands on the street side of the square, and is a metallic structure measuring 37 metres (121 ft) in height.

facts.fact: A museum for Fuku Akino's work was built in her hometown of Hamamatsu in 1998, designed by Terunobu Fujimori.
facts.quote: A museum housing her artworks was built in her hometown of Hamamatsu in 1998. The museum was designed by Japanese architect Terunobu Fujimori.

facts.fact: Fujimori lists it among his works: Fuku Akino Art Museum (1998), Hamamatsu.
facts.quote: Fuku Akino Art Museum (1998), Hamamatsu City, Shizuoka Prefecture

facts.fact: Fuku Akino was a Japanese painter known for paintings of Indian themes, landscapes and peoples.
facts.quote: Fuku Akino (秋野 不矩, Akino Fuku; July 25, 1908 - October 11, 2001) was a Japanese painter. She was born in  Futamata, Iwata-gun, Shizuoka Prefecture (currently, Nimata Town, Tenryu Ward, Hamamatsu City). She became known by her paintings of Indian themes, landscapes and peoples.

facts.fact: The Municipal Building is a 40-storey, 580-foot building at 1 Centre Street in Manhattan's Civic Center.
facts.quote: The David N. Dinkins Municipal Building (originally the Municipal Building and later known as the Manhattan Municipal Building) is a 40-story, 580-foot (180 m) building at 1 Centre Street, east of Chambers Street, in the Civic Center neighborhood of Manhattan in New York City, United States.

facts.fact: It was built for the extra government space needed after New York's five boroughs were consolidated in 1898.
facts.quote: The structure was built to accommodate increased governmental space demands after the 1898 consolidation of the city's five boroughs. Construction began in 1909 and continued through 1914 at a total cost of $12 million (equivalent to $284,515,000 in 2025).

facts.fact: William M. Kendall of McKim, Mead & White designed the building.
facts.quote: William M. Kendall of the architectural firm McKim, Mead & White designed the Municipal Building.

facts.fact: It was among the last buildings of the City Beautiful movement in New York.
facts.quote: Designed by McKim, Mead & White, the Manhattan Municipal Building was among the last buildings erected as part of the City Beautiful movement in New York.

facts.fact: It was the first building in New York City to incorporate a subway station below its base.
facts.quote: The Municipal Building was the first in New York City to incorporate a subway station, the Chambers Street station, below its base.

facts.fact: In plan the building is a ten-sided 'C', set on an irregular hexagonal lot.
facts.quote: The building is shaped like a ten-sided "C", although the lot that it occupies is an irregular hexagon.

facts.fact: The C-shaped floor plan gave every window direct sunlight and removed the need for an interior light court.
facts.quote: This floor plan ensured that all of the building's windows would be able to receive direct sunlight and eliminated the need for an interior light court.

facts.fact: The façade is ashlar granite, with a three-storey Corinthian colonnade along Centre Street.
facts.quote: The facade is made of ashlar granite, except for the details above the 23rd floor, which are made of terracotta. A three-story colonnade of Corinthian columns runs across the base along Centre Street, and the rest of the building is set back behind the colonnade.

facts.fact: It is topped by Adolph Weinman's gilded copper statue Civic Fame, 25 feet tall, installed in 1913.
facts.quote: On the Municipal Building's roof is Civic Fame, a 25-foot-tall (7.6 m) statue installed in March 1913. The statue is a gilded copper figure, made from about 500 pieces of hammered copper executed by the Manhattan firm of Broschart & Braun.

facts.fact: It became a New York City landmark in 1966 and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.
facts.quote: The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the building a landmark in 1966, and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.

facts.fact: Oscar Niemeyer's Church of Our Lady of Fatima, known as the Igrejinha of 307/308 Sul, dates from 1958.
facts.quote: 1958 – Church of Our Lady of Fatima ("Igrejinha Nossa Senhora de Fátima"/"A Igrejinha da 307/308 Sul")

facts.fact: The Chicago Board of Trade Building is a 44-storey, 604-foot Art Deco skyscraper at the foot of the LaSalle Street 'canyon' in the Loop.
facts.quote: The Chicago Board of Trade Building is a 44-story, 604-foot (184 m) Art Deco skyscraper located in the Chicago Loop, standing at the foot of the LaSalle Street "canyon".

facts.fact: It replaced an earlier building on the site and was designed by Holabird & Root; it was Chicago's tallest until 1965.
facts.quote: The Boyington building became unsound in the 1920s and was demolished in 1929, replaced by the current building designed by Holabird & Root. The current building was itself Chicago's tallest until 1965, when it was surpassed by the Richard J. Daley Center.

facts.fact: Clad in grey Indiana limestone and topped with a copper pyramid roof, it opened on 9 June 1930.
facts.quote: Clad in gray Indiana limestone, topped with a copper pyramid roof, and standing on a site running 174 ft (53 m) east–west on Jackson Boulevard and 240 ft (73 m) north–south on LaSalle Street, the 605 ft (184 m) tall art deco-styled building opened on June 9, 1930.

facts.fact: Its fourth floor held what was then the world's largest trading floor.
facts.quote: The Chicago Board of Trade has operated continuously on its fourth floor since the 1930 opening, dedicating 19,000 square feet (1,800 m2) to what was then the world's largest trading floor.

facts.fact: Its setbacks let more light into the deepening street 'valleys', and are floodlit at night to stress the vertical lines.
facts.quote: The advent of steel frame structural systems allowed completely vertical construction; but as with many skyscrapers of the era, the exterior was designed with multiple setbacks at increasing heights, which served to allow additional light into the ever-deepening concrete "valleys" in urban cores. At night, the setbacks are upwardly lit by floodlights, further emphasizing the structure's vertical elements.

facts.fact: The interior has polished surfaces, black and white marble and a three-storey lobby.
facts.quote: Interior decoration includes polished surfaces throughout, the use of black and white marble, prominent vertical hallway trim, and an open three-story lobby which at the time of opening housed the world's largest electric light fixture.

facts.fact: A 31-foot aluminium statue of Ceres, Roman goddess of grain, by John H. Storrs caps the building.
facts.quote: The central structure is capped by a 6,500 pound, 31 ft (9.4 m) tall aluminum statue by sculptor John H. Storrs of the Roman goddess of grain, Ceres, holding a sheaf of wheat in the left hand and a bag of corn in the right hand, as a nod to the exchange's heritage as a commodities market.

facts.fact: It became a Chicago Landmark in 1977 and a National Historic Landmark in 1978.
facts.quote: The building was listed as a Chicago Landmark in 1977 and a National Historic Landmark and National Register of Historic Places honoree in 1978.

facts.fact: Christian de Portzamparc designed the Tour de Lille, built 1991–1995.
facts.quote: 1991–1995 Tour de Lille, Lille

facts.fact: McKim was asked to design the Boston Public Library in 1887; its completion in 1895 brought the firm new institutional clients.
facts.quote: Their status rose when McKim was asked to design the Boston Public Library in 1887, ensuring a new group of institutional clients following its successful completion in 1895.

facts.fact: The library (1888–95) exemplifies McKim's Beaux-Arts architecture in the styles of the American Renaissance.
facts.quote: McKim became best known as an exponent of Beaux-Arts architecture in styles of the American Renaissance, exemplified by the Boston Public Library (1888–95), and several works in New York City.

facts.fact: Edward Lippincott Tilton helped design the library in 1890.
facts.quote: Edward Lippincott Tilton – helped design the Boston Public Library in 1890 before leaving with Boring.

facts.fact: By then the firm was drawing on French, Renaissance and Roman buildings as sources for new work.
facts.quote: The firm had begun to use classical sources from Modern French, Renaissance and even Roman buildings as sources of inspiration for daring new work.

facts.fact: Lappia Hall is a performing arts venue and conference centre in Rovaniemi, Lapland, near the Arctic Circle, designed by Alvar Aalto.
facts.quote: Lappia Hall (Finnish: Lappia-talo) is a performing arts venue and conference centre in Rovaniemi, the capital city of the Finnish Lapland region, situated close to the Arctic Circle. It is notable for having been designed by the renowned Finnish architect Alvar Aalto in the modernist style.

facts.fact: Its wavy roofline recalls the fells of Lapland.
facts.quote: The wavy exterior roofline is reminiscent of the fells of Lapland.

facts.fact: The interior uses light wood and plain white surfaces with blue accents, typical of late Aalto, with Artek lights and furniture.
facts.quote: The interior design makes extensive use of light wood and plain white surfaces with blue accents, typical of Aalto's later work. The public areas are largely furnished with light fixtures and furniture by Aalto's own furniture and interior design company, Artek.

facts.fact: It was built in phases finished in 1961, 1971 and 1975, and was the last building Aalto saw completed.
facts.quote: The second phase, completed in 1971, is home to the municipal Rovaniemi Theatre, while the final phase, the conference centre, was finished in 1975. Lappia Hall was the last building Aalto saw finished, before his death in 1976.

facts.fact: It was renovated and expanded in 2013–2015 and now has three auditoriums seating about 600 in all.
facts.quote: In 2013–2015, the interior of the building was extensively renovated, as well as expanded to include underground performance venue and service areas. Today, the building comprises three auditoriums with a total seating capacity of c. 600, as well as two restaurants.

facts.fact: With the library and city hall it forms Aalto's 'Aalto Centre', protected as a nationally important built environment.
facts.quote: Lappia Hall forms part of a wider complex of public and administrative buildings designed by Aalto, known collectively as the 'Aalto Centre', along with the adjacent Rovaniemi library (completed in 1965) and Rovaniemi city hall (1988). The complex has been designated and protected by the Finnish Heritage Agency as a nationally important built cultural environment (Valtakunnallisesti merkittävä rakennettu kulttuuriympäristö).

facts.fact: The original Berkeley Art Museum, by Mario Ciampi with Ronald Wagner and Richard Jurasch, came from a 1964 competition and opened in 1970.
facts.quote: A competition to design a building was announced in 1964, and the museum, designed by Mario Ciampi, and associates Ronald Wagner and Richard Jurasch, opened in 1970.

facts.fact: The concrete Brutalist building, one of the most inventive in that style, has a fan-shaped procession down a spiral of semi-open galleries; it was judged seismically unsafe in 1997 and braced in 2001.
facts.quote: The concrete Brutalist structure—one of the most inventive buildings in that style, with its fan-shaped procession down a spiral of semi-open galleries—was deemed seismically unsafe in 1997, and iron braces were added in 2001 to improve safety.

facts.fact: Ciampi won the AIACC 25-Year Award for it in 1996.
facts.quote: Ciampi won AIACC's 25-Year Award in 1996 for the Berkeley Art Museum.

facts.fact: The City of Berkeley declared it a landmark in 2012.
facts.quote: The City of Berkeley declared it to be a landmark in 2012.

facts.fact: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2014.
facts.quote: The vacated Mario Ciampi building was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2014.

facts.fact: Retrofitted, it reopened in late 2021 as the Bakar BioEnginuity Hub, a biotech incubator.
facts.quote: The building, seismically retrofitted and "reimagined", reopened in late 2021 as the Bakar BioEnginuity Hub, an incubator for biotechnology start-ups, named Woo Hon Fai Hall in honor of the father of a donor, David Woo.

facts.fact: It is a Catholic minor basilica in Yamoussoukro, the administrative capital of Ivory Coast, listed by Guinness as the largest church in the world.
facts.quote: The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace (French: Basilique Notre-Dame de la Paix, pronounced [bazilik nɔtʁə dam də la pɛ]) is a Catholic minor basilica dedicated to Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro, the administrative capital of Ivory Coast. Guinness World Records lists it as the largest church in the world, having surpassed the previous record holder, Saint Peter's Basilica, upon completion.

facts.fact: It covers 30,000 m² (including a rectory and villa) and is 158 m tall, holding 18,000 worshippers.
